overlap.title: Elijah “went up … into heaven”, or “no man hath ascended up to heaven”?
overlap.summary: 2 Kings says Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven. John says no man has ascended up to heaven except the Son of man. The Greek of 2 Kings says Elijah was taken up “as it were” into heaven.
overlap.reasoning: The KJV and the Hebrew of 2 Kings say that Elijah went up into heaven. John has Jesus say that no man has gone up to heaven but the one who came down from it. As worded, the second statement leaves no room for the first. Brenton’s Greek of 2 Kings twice has a word the KJV lacks, “as it were” into heaven, in the verse itself and in the chapter’s opening line.
overlap.scope: G applies at 2 Kings 2:11 only: the Septuagint Greek there qualifies “into heaven” and the KJV does not. In John the KJV matches the Greek New Testament. The two KJV statements can both stand if “heaven” in Kings means the sky and in John the dwelling of God, or if John speaks only of one who went up and came back to report; neither book says so. The record does not decide why the Greek has “as it were”. The Textus Receptus digital text prints no accents; Tischendorf’s edition was also compared, and no other Greek New Testament edition was. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. overlap.title: Jehoram of Israel: king from the second year of Jehoram of Judah, or the eighteenth of Jehoshaphat?
overlap.summary: 2 Kings 1:17 dates Jehoram of Israel from the second year of Jehoram of Judah. 3:1 dates him from the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat, and 8:16 has Jehoram of Judah begin in the fifth year of Jehoram of Israel. The Greek of 1:17 has no date.
overlap.reasoning: By 1:17 Jehoram of Judah was already in his second year when Jehoram of Israel began. By 8:16 Jehoram of Judah began in the fifth year of Jehoram of Israel. Each king is made to begin after the other. 3:1 gives a third date for the same accession, under the father, Jehoshaphat. Brenton’s Greek has no date in 1:17 and gives only the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat, in a verse the KJV lacks.
overlap.scope: G applies at 2 Kings 1:17 only, where the Greek lacks the date the KJV has. The three KJV dates fit if Jehoram of Judah was made king beside his father some years before he reigned alone; the words “Jehoshaphat being then king of Judah” in 8:16 may point that way, but no verse reports two accessions. overlap.title: Josiah’s death: slain at Megiddo and carried away dead, or brought wounded to Jerusalem, where he died?
overlap.summary: 2 Kings says Pharaoh slew Josiah at Megiddo and his servants carried him dead from there. 2 Chronicles says he was wounded, moved to another chariot and brought to Jerusalem, “and he died”.
overlap.reasoning: Kings places the death at Megiddo and has a dead man carried to Jerusalem. Chronicles has a wounded man speak, be moved, and be brought to Jerusalem, and only then says he died.
overlap.scope: No tag is proposed: the KJV matches the Hebrew in both books, and the Greek agrees in each. Chronicles does not say in so many words where Josiah died; the order of its clauses puts the death after the journey. If the Hebrew word rendered “dead” in Kings is taken as “dying”, the accounts draw closer; the record does not decide that, and verse 29 still says he was put to death at Megiddo. overlap.title: Which kings of Egypt were the Pharaohs of the oppression and the exodus?
overlap.summary: Exodus tells of a new king who knew not Joseph, of his death, and of the Pharaoh whom Moses faced, and names none of them. Later books name kings of Egypt. Which king oppressed Israel, and which let them go, is not stated.
overlap.reasoning: The story turns on at least two kings: the one who began the oppression and died, and the one who refused Moses and then let Israel go. Each is called only “the king of Egypt” or “Pharaoh”. Who they were decides when the events are placed and against which Egyptian records they can be compared, so the gap is a material one. It is not that the books never name Egyptian kings: Shishak, Pharaohnechoh and Pharaohhophra are named in Kings and Jeremiah.
overlap.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. That the two kings can be identified from the city name Raamses at 1:11, or from the 480 years of 1 Kings 6:1 counted back from Solomon, are both readings; they lead to different kings, and neither passage names one. This record asserts neither. Check made for an answer elsewhere: the packaged KJV was searched for “Pharaoh” joined to a further name and for the words Shishak, So king, and Tirhakah; the verses found are in Kings, Chronicles, Isaiah and Jeremiah and concern later centuries. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible, and it does not prove that no passage addresses the question. No G is proposed: at 1:8 Brenton’s Greek has “another king” where the KJV has “a new king”, a difference too slight to tag. No claim is made about Egyptian history.
